Gareth: Hi Tammy! I haven't seen you in such a long time!
Tammy: Yeah, ever since my twin sister and your best friend broke up.
Gareth: A best friend will be unpredictable sometimes.
Tammy: He sent a Valentine's message to his ex-girlfriend.
Gareth: Can you believe that? Frank would do something like that, wouldn't he? It's so typical of him! That might explain why she broke up with him.
Tammy: Ah yeah ... just a little.
Gareth: In any case, it wasn't my fault, right? I'm sure we will still get along like before.
Tammy: I guess. A sister will do what she has to do.
Gareth: What have you been up to these days?

Tammy: I've been looking for a job, but it's been really hard. I get shy in interviews.
Gareth: I know what you're saying. I have something you might be interested in.
Tammy: What is it?
Gareth: I have decided to join the local Toastmaster's Club. It's a group that helps you practice public speaking. I believe that it will help me build my confidence for speaking in public.
Tammy: My neighbor used to do that. He would practice his speeches every evening. That explains why it looked like he was talking to himself. What do people talk about?
Gareth: The speeches are unpredictable. It's up to each individual to prepare their own speech. I haven't decided what to talk about yet.

Tammy: It takes a courageous person to speak in front of a group of strangers like that.
Gareth: After your speech, there is a short period for questions and answers.
Tammy: I suspect it must be difficult to prepare for that.
Gareth: Yes, you never know what someone might ask you. The question could be only indirectly related to your topic. You have to be very adaptable. You should try it!
Tammy: I don't know!

In speaking, you often use wh-words to ask information questions. These words can also be used to begin a clause after certain verbs.
These wh-words can be pronouns (who, whom, whose, what, which, that) or adverbs (when, where, why, how). That is sometimes used in place of which or who.
Some verbs that can be followed by wh-words are:

Examples:
I didn't understand what I saw in the YouTube video because the images were so blurry.
I forgot my lunch and only remembered when I had already arrived at school.

You could also use many of these verbs with a that-clause or a wh-clause + infinitive (to + verb).
The wh-clause + infinitive cannot be used with why. Also, you don't use an infinitive if there is a subject in the wh-clause.

Examples:
Every time I saw the scar on my forehead, I remembered that I fell off the swing.

Julia couldn't decide which dress to wear to the graduation party.
My boyfriend is quite blunt and always says what he thinks.
I haven't decided what to talk about yet.
Modals to Describe Present and Past Habits
You can talk about habits in the present and the past using special modal verbs like will, would and used to. These modals are followed by the simple form of the verb (the infinitive with “to”).

One way of talking about present habits is to use the Present Simple.
I brush my teeth every night before I go to bed.
You can also use will to talk about habits and routines. Will can also be used to talk about how something naturally acts or the characteristics of a person.

• My brother will always go to the Bahamas on vacation. He likes tropical weather and relaxing on the beach. (habit or routine)
  • A good doctor will try to make a patient feel comfortable. (characteristic)
  • Dogs will bark when they sense danger. (natural behavior)
If you want to express your annoyance about a habit, you can use will, will not or won't. In speaking, you need to place more stress on the not in the negative will not.

• My grandmother will always insist that I eat something even if I'm not hungry.
  • My friend will not quit smoking even though he knows it's bad for his health.

Used to is for past habits or states. You would probably use this expression most often when talking about your childhood or when you were younger. This is for states or routines that happened frequently in the past. It also means that the habit or state has changed and that you no longer do this action. Because you can use used to for states and habits, it can be followed by action verbs and stative verbs.

• I used to go to ballet lessons every Thursday. (action verb)
  • I used to hate eating broccoli when I was a child. (stative verb)
For negatives and questions, the form of used to is different.

• I didn't use to go to the gym in university.
  • Did you use to like cartoons when you were younger?
You can use would for recurring actions in the past as well. However, this cannot be used with past states, and is only used with action verbs. This is often shortened to 'd in speaking.

• I would go to ballet lessons every Thursday. (action verb)
  • I used to hate eating broccoli when I was a child. (stative verb, so cannot use would)
